resources.title: Introduction to Chemistry - Expanded Instructional Note
resources.content: Definition, History, Branches, and Importance DEFINITION OF CHEMISTRY Chemistry is the branch of science that deals with the study of the composition, structure, properties, and changes (reactions) of matter. It seeks to understand:  What matter is made of (composition)  How matter is arranged (structure)  How matter behaves (properties)  How matter changes (chemical reactions) Chemistry is often called the “central science” because it connects and overlaps with other sciences like Physics, Biology, Medicine, and Geology. HISTORY OF CHEMISTRY The history of chemistry can be divided into several stages: a. Ancient Period (Before 16th Century)  Early humans used natural substances such as fire, salt, and metals like gold and copper without understanding their composition.  The practice of alchemy emerged, combining elements of magic, religion, and early experimentation.  Alchemists sought to transform base metals (like lead) into gold and to discover the elixir of life. b. Transition Period (16th–18th Century)  The idea of experimentation and observation started replacing mystical beliefs.  Robert Boyle (1627–1691) is regarded as the father of modern chemistry for his emphasis on experimentation and his famous Boyle’s Law on gases.  Antoine Lavoisier (1743–1794), called the father of modern chemistry, named “oxygen” and “hydrogen, ” and established the Law of Conservation of Mass. c. Modern Period (19th Century – Present)  Development of the Atomic Theory by John Dalton (1808).  Discovery of the Periodic Table by Dmitri Mendeleev (1869).  Advancements in physical chemistry, organic chemistry, and biochemistry.  In the 20th century, chemistry expanded into nuclear chemistry, polymer chemistry, and analytical chemistry. BRANCHES OF CHEMISTRY Chemistry is broadly divided into the following branches: a. Physical Chemistry Deals with the physical properties and behavior of matter, energy changes, and reaction rates. Examples: study of thermodynamics, chemical equilibrium, and kinetics. b. Organic Chemistry Study of compounds containing carbon (except carbonates and oxides of carbon). Examples: hydrocarbons, alcohols, and plastics. c. Inorganic Chemistry Study of elements and compounds that are not based on carbon. Examples: metals, salts, and minerals. d. Analytical Chemistry Focuses on methods used to determine the composition of substances (qualitative and quantitative analysis). Examples: titration, spectroscopy, chromatography. e. Biochemistry Study of chemical processes in living organisms. Examples: digestion, respiration, and photosynthesis. f. Industrial Chemistry Application of chemical principles in industries to produce useful materials such as fertilizers, paints, drugs, and soaps. IMPORTANCE OF CHEMISTRY Chemistry plays a vital role in everyday life and national development. a. In Medicine and Health  Production of drugs, vaccines, and anesthetics.  Development of disinfectants and diagnostic chemicals. b. In Agriculture  Manufacture of fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides.  Development of soil analysis and irrigation chemicals. c. In Industry  Production of plastics, paints, soap, cement, textiles, and cosmetics.  Extraction and purification of metals. d. In Environment  Helps to understand and control pollution.  Development of renewable energy sources. e. In Food and Nutrition  Preservation and processing of food.  Production of flavorings and supplements. f. In Scientific Research  Provides a foundation for innovations in energy, materials, and biotechnology.
